absent: Fresh folio allocation path, node retry mask handling and preparation steps beyond their call sites.
Bulk freeing path and reservation accounting updates outside the observed counter adjustments.
Size lookup, size iteration, gigantic classification and contiguous reservation size helpers.
Fault-mutex usage during page faults and reservation or unmapping interactions.
Sysfs attribute semantics, demote interface behavior and sysctl table contents.
Cgroup template contents and controller charge semantics.
Early boot gigantic initialization and bootmem node setup.
Vmemmap optimization thresholds, restore behavior and high-memory classification.
Definitions of node states, first memory node and NUMA helpers.

findings.text: A cross-size demotion service accepts a source size descriptor, a node constraint and a desired count, moves free folios toward the configured smaller size, and reports the moved count or a negative failure indicator.

A numeric store handler validates gigantic sizing capability, derives a node constraint from request scope and current memory policy, delegates pool resizing, and reports request length on success or a negative error otherwise.

Boot-time size registration ensures one descriptor per page order, initializes its sizing lock, order, mask, free lists, active list, printable name and parse cursor, and silently ignores an already present order.
Per-node sysfs lifecycle hooks create a node-level container and one child per size on registration, and remove children plus container on unregistration, tolerating absent or already present state.

Early setup exposes distinct initializers for global sysfs, cgroup files and sysctl entries, plus a weak architecture hook for size validity that defaults to accepting only the built-in default huge page size.

Each size descriptor selects a demote target order equal to the largest smaller configured order, except gigantic sizes without runtime freeing and small sizes under platform contiguous reservation support keep a zero target meaning no demotion.

Persistent pool size is total pages minus surplus pages, and the stored maximum tracks that persistent value after resizing or demotion, with demotion scaling the destination maximum by the size ratio between source and destination orders.

Surplus adjustment moves the global and one node-local surplus counter together by exactly one step, choosing a node that can absorb the change under the supplied node constraint and reporting success or inability.
Gigantic sizes face growth restrictions when large contiguous allocation support or runtime freeing support is absent, while shrinking remains permitted in the observed paths.
Size identity combines an allocation order with an address mask derived from the corresponding byte size, and a stable printable name derived from that size.

Policy-derived node constraints copy the task policy node set for bind-like and interleave-like modes, use the executing node for local mode, and report absence when no task policy or mask is present.

Cgroup file generation builds one concrete entry per template entry per size, combining a human size label with the template name, packing size index with template identity, and striding offset entries by size index.

A size with no demote target exposes only its base attribute group, while a size with a nonzero demote target additionally exposes a demote attribute group whose creation failure tears down the whole size entry.

Pool resizing serializes callers with a per-size sizing mutex and protects counters and free lists with a global spin lock with interrupt exclusion, releasing the spin lock across fresh allocation, bulk freeing and scheduling points.

Demotion requires the global pool spin lock on entry for selection and accounting, releases it while splitting folios without locks held, then reacquires it before requeueing leftovers and updating maxima.

Splitting into a destination size acquires the destination sizing mutex while already holding the source sizing mutex, following a larger-size-first order to avoid deadlock and to prevent concurrent resizing from converting arriving pages to surplus.
Low-memory reclamation assumes the global pool spin lock is held, collects candidates under that lock, then drops it for bulk freeing and reacquires it before returning to the caller.
Reading current task memory policy for node-mask derivation happens under the task lock, and fault handling uses a boot-allocated table of mutexes whose count scales with possible processor count.

A huge-page size descriptor carries order and demote order, global and per-node total, surplus, free, reserved and maximum counts, next allocation and free node cursors, per-node free lists, an active list, a sizing mutex, mask, order index and printable name.
Per-node sysfs state holds a node-level object plus one child object per size, indexed by size position, supporting idempotent creation and ordered teardown of demote, base and parent objects.

Cgroup file storage consists of two boot-allocated arrays sized by size count times template count plus terminator, one for default hierarchy and one for legacy hierarchy, later registered with the controller subsystem.

Pool growth first absorbs surplus pages, then allocates fresh folios one at a time with rescheduling and signal checks, stages them locally, and publishes them to the pool before any shrinking phase begins.

Pool shrinking first preserves enough persistent pages for reservations by computing free persistent pages and a floor, frees selected free pages outside the lock, then converts remaining excess persistent pages into surplus for later release.

Free-folio demotion restores optimized mappings, skips still-optimized folios, splits each remaining source folio into destination-sized folios while preserving contiguous-reservation marking, and publishes the new folios to the destination pool.

Node-scoped demotion iterates allowed nodes, detaches up to the remaining requested non-poisoned free folios per node, demotes them without the pool lock, requeues unprocessed leftovers, and stops on error, completion or list exhaustion.

Boot setup checks platform support, guarantees the default size entry, resolves default size and counts including per-node maxima, initializes all sizes, reports them, initializes user interfaces, and finally allocates and initializes the fault-mutex table.

User-interface setup creates a global container and one entry per size, marks per-node support ready where applicable, registers every online node, and leaves global setup silent when the top container cannot be created.

The subsystem boot entry point performs support checks, default-size resolution, size initialization and reporting, interface registration, and fault-mutex table allocation, returning success even when huge pages are unsupported.
Node-specific resize arithmetic can wrap on very large requested counts, and the implementation clamps such wrap to the largest representable value to honor an allocate-as-much-as-possible intent.

Growth aborts promptly on pending signals after publishing already staged pages, allocation failure publishes staged pages and ends growth, and surplus conversion races may leave the pool transiently larger than requested.
Demotion rejects a missing target order as an internal error, skips poisoned source pages, leaves optimized folios with the source, and reports busy when only poisoned pages prevented any progress.
Low-memory reclamation ignores gigantic sizes entirely in one build variant and ignores high-memory folios during collection, stopping once the retained pool would reach the requested floor.

Size entries use a kilobyte-based printable label for sysfs and cgroup size prefixes use gigabyte, megabyte or kilobyte suffix selection by magnitude, with concrete file names joining that prefix and template name by a separator.
Cgroup file identity packs size index in upper bits with template identity in lower bits, while offset entries encode base offset in upper bits and per-size stride in lower bits.
The fault-mutex table contains one mutex in single-processor builds and otherwise a power-of-two rounding of eight times the possible processor count.
